How to Use an Electric Beard Trimmer for a Jaunty or Playful Beard Style

Step 1: Choose the Right Trimmer
First things first, choose an electric beard trimmer that suits your beard length, texture, and style preferences. Select a trimmer with adjustable settings and a minimum of three different trimming combs.

Step 2: Prepare Your Beard
Before you start trimming, make sure your beard is dry and clean. Wash your beard with a mild shampoo and towel-dry it thoroughly. If you have a long beard, brush it out gently with a wide-tooth comb to remove any tangles or knots.

Step 3: Set the Trimmer
Attach the desired trimming comb to the trimmer and set the trimming length. You can start with a longer length setting and gradually reduce it as you go. Remember, it's always better to trim less and gradually than to cut too much in one go.

Step 4: Trim the Beard
Start trimming your beard by running the trimmer along your beard hairs in the direction of their growth. Keep the trimmer steady and move it slowly and carefully around the contours of your face. Use a mirror to check that you are trimming evenly and not missing any spots.

Step 5: Create Symmetry
To create a symmetrical beard shape, divide your beard into sections and trim each section individually. For example, trim the sides first, then the chin, then the mustache, and then the cheeks. Use a smaller trimmer comb size and trim the sides, bottom, and under your chin.

Step 6: Shape the Beard
Once you have trimmed the beard, it's time to shape it. Use the edge of the trimmer without a comb attachment to create clean and straight lines around the edges of your beard. You can also create texture by using the trimmer to cut in different directions or shapes.

Step 7: Maintain the Beard
Keep your beard looking great by trimming it regularly. Depending on the length, you may need to trim it every week or two to keep it looking neat and tidy. Use a beard oil to keep your beard and skin moisturized.

Safety Precautions:
- Always read the manual and follow the manufacturer's instructions.
- Make sure the trimmer is unplugged before cleaning or changing attachments.
- Do not use the trimmer on wet hair or in wet conditions.
- Keep the trimmer away from children and pets.

Product Recommendations:

- Wahl Lithium Ion Plus Beard Trimmer
- Remington PG6025 All-in-1 Lithium Powered Grooming Kit

Troubleshooting Tips:
- If your beard trimmer is not cutting effectively, the blades may be dull. Replace the blades or sharpen them if possible.
- If your trimmer is pulling on your beard hairs, make sure you are using the right comb attachment or adjusting the length setting accordingly.
- If you experience any discomfort or irritation while trimming, stop and seek medical advice.

One of his first jobs was as an illustrator for Liwayway Publications, where he worked with people like Ang Kiukok and Alfredo Roces. He later took job with the United States Information Service as a layout artist, followed by stints at Mirror Magazine and the Sunday Times Magazine.
In 1966, he held his first solo exhibition at the Gallery Indigo in Mabini, where he introduced the iconic subject Sabel, a madwoman and scavenger which would dominate and permeate throughout his creative life.
Marriage to British writer Caroline Kennedy relocated Bencab to London, where he found fame and fortune, eventually earning a reputation as one of if not the well-received painter of his generation of Filipino artists.

As soon as Emily walked into her new home, she felt a sense of unease. The place felt cold and unwelcoming, despite the bright walls and large windows. But she had fallen in love with the house's Victorian charm, the creaky floorboards, and the spacious rooms. It was perfect.

But as she began to unpack her things, Emily noticed something strange. There was a doorway seemingly leading to nowhere, hidden in one of the corners of the living room. She tried to open it, but it wouldn't budge. Emily brushed it off as some odd quirk of an old house and continued settling in.

That was until one night, she heard a haunting sound coming from behind the door. It sounded like whispers, like an unknown language spoken by a group of disembodied voices. Emily felt a chill run up her spine, but she dismissed it as her imagination running wild.

However, the following night, the sounds returned, louder and more distinct this time. Emily couldn't ignore it anymore, so she gathered all her courage and decided to investigate.

She tried to open the door again, but it was locked. After some fiddling and twisting, the lock finally gave way. The room was pitch black, and Emily fumbled around for a switch. When she finally found it, the light flickered on, and that's when Emily wished she had never opened the door.

The room was empty, other than the countless mirrors all around her. The walls were lined with floor-to-ceiling mirrors, and in the center of the room was a strange altar, draped in pitch-black robes, surrounded by candles. Emily felt a sense of dread and unease she had never experienced before.

As Emily took a step into the room, she saw a figure entering the mirrors' reflection behind her. She turned around, and for some reason, the figure wasn't present. She continued to explore the room, but something inside of her had changed. Her thoughts started to race, and she felt herself going insane.

That's when she heard a voice, a low, menacing voice, whispering into her ear, "You shouldn't have opened the door." Emily screamed and ran out of the room, slamming the door shut behind her.

After that night, Emily could never bring herself to enter that room again. She sold the house soon after, never looking back. But every night, she hears the whispers, and every night she prays to forget the image of the mirrors and the black-robed altar. Emily understands that some things shouldn't be discovered, that sometimes, it's better to leave well enough alone.

Introduction

Email marketing is one of the most effective forms of digital marketing, and its relevance has continued to grow as more businesses and individuals use email as an important means of communication. Email marketing is a cost-effective way to reach potential and existing customers, communicate with them, and build relationships. Sending emails with personalized content, targeting specific segments of customers, and using clear calls-to-action can lead to increased engagement and conversions. In this report, we will discuss the best practices for email marketing and provide recommendations for content, style, frequency, segmentation, personalization, subject lines, and calls-to-action. We will also share case studies and examples of successful email campaigns.

Content

The content of your emails is one of the most critical elements of your email marketing strategy. Your email should be engaging, informative, and relevant to your audience. This includes providing value to your readers through useful information and helpful tips, promotions and discounts, and exclusive content.

Use catchy headlines and subheadings throughout your email to grab the recipient's attention quickly. Be sure to use short paragraphs and bullet points to break up the content and make it more digestible. You should also use images and videos to make your emails more visually appealing.

Style

Your emails should be visually appealing, easy to read, and consistent with your brand's style and voice. Using different fonts, colors, and images can help you make an impact and keep readers interested.

Avoid using too many different colors or excessive formatting that can make your email look cluttered or unprofessional. Keep your design clean, simple, and consistent.

Frequency

The frequency of your emails should depend on your business, audience, and goals. You don't want to bombard your readers with too many emails, or they may quickly unsubscribe. However, you also don't want to create too much space between communications, as you may lose touch with your audience.

Create a schedule that works for your business and stick to it. You can also send targeted emails based on specific events or promotions relevant to your audience.

Segmentation

Segmenting your email list allows you to target specific groups of customers with personalized content. This segmentation can be based on demographics, behavior, location, or other factors.

For example, if you own a clothing store, you might segment your email list into different groups based on gender or age. This allows you to send targeted emails with product recommendations and promotions that are more relevant to the recipient.

Personalization

Personalizing your emails can help increase engagement and customer loyalty. Use the recipient's name, previous purchase history, and other information to tailor your email content to their interests and needs.

For example, if a customer has previously purchased a specific product, you can send them an email with recommendations for similar products. This not only provides value to the customer but also increases the likelihood of them making another purchase.

Subject Lines

Your email subject line is one of the most critical elements of your email campaign. It should be short and attention-grabbing to encourage the recipient to open your email.

Avoid using click-bait or misleading subject lines that may cause your emails to be marked as spam. Instead, use clear and concise language that describes the content of your email.

Calls-to-Action

Your email should have a clear call-to-action that encourages the recipient to take some action. This can be anything from making a purchase to signing up for a newsletter or following you on social media.

Your call-to-action should be prominently placed in your email and use clear language that tells the recipient exactly what you want them to do. Adding urgency or scarcity to your call-to-action can increase the likelihood of them taking action.

Case Study: Airbnb

Airbnb uses email marketing to communicate with existing and potential customers. They use segmentation to target specific groups of customers with personalized content.

In one example, they sent an email to users who had not booked a trip in a while. The email used personalized content and subject lines to encourage users to book a trip. The email had a clear call-to-action to encourage users to take action, and the email resulted in a 400% increase in bookings.

Case Study: HubSpot

HubSpot uses email marketing to communicate with potential customers and promote their business software. They use personalized content and segmentation to target specific groups of customers.

In one example, they sent an email to users who had recently downloaded one of their ebooks. The email provided personalized content with helpful tips and links to additional resources. The email had a clear call-to-action to encourage users to schedule a demo, resulting in a 21% conversion rate.

Conclusion

Email marketing is an essential part of any digital marketing strategy, and its effectiveness depends on the quality of your email content, style, frequency, segmentation, personalization, subject lines, and calls-to-action. By using these best practices, you can increase engagement and conversions among your email subscribers. Remember to measure your email campaign's success through analytics data and adjust your strategy accordingly.

Traditional Japanese cuisine, also known as washoku, has a long history and has evolved over many centuries. Here is a brief overview of its history and evolution:

Pre-12th century:

Before the 12th century, the food culture in Japan was heavily influenced by neighboring countries like China and Korea. Rice was the staple food, and its cultivation played an important role in shaping the food culture of Japan. The early Japanese diet also included fish, vegetables, and wild game.

12th century-Edo period (1603-1868):

During this period, Japan experienced significant changes in its cuisine. The development of the Buddhist temples and tea ceremonies led to the creation of new cooking techniques and styles. The food culture became more sophisticated and diverse, with regional cuisines developing across the country.

In the Edo period, the samurai class emerged as the elite, and their diet was dominated by meat and fish, which were expensive and only available to the wealthy. Street food and fast food also became popular in urban areas, with food stalls and stands selling a variety of snack foods like sushi, yakitori, and fried tofu.

Meiji period (1868-1912):

The Meiji period marked a significant turning point in Japan's history, with the opening of the country to the West. This resulted in an influx of foreign influences, including food. Western-style cooking techniques and dishes like bread, cheese, and butter were introduced to Japan.

However, the Japanese government began to promote traditional Japanese cuisine as a way to preserve the country's culture and identity. The first Japanese cookbook was published during this period, and restaurants serving traditional Japanese cuisine began to appear across the country.

Post-World War II:

After World War II, Japan experienced a rapid economic growth, which resulted in changes in the food culture. The introduction of new appliances like refrigerators and rice cookers made cooking easier and more convenient. This led to an increase in the consumption of convenience foods and fast food.

However, traditional Japanese cuisine continued to be revered and promoted as a symbol of Japan's cultural heritage. In 2013, washoku was added to UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

Today, traditional Japanese cuisine remains popular both within Japan and across the world. It emphasizes fresh, seasonal ingredients, simple presentation, and a balance of flavors. The popularity of washoku has also led to the emergence of fusion cuisine, where chefs combine traditional Japanese ingredients with Western cooking techniques and flavors.

prompt:
How can leaders equip their team to navigate the hidden curriculum of work? Answer according to: Official job descriptions don’t include the most valuable contributions you make or the complicated challenges you face.
What do you do for work? Not, what is your job title, or what’s written in your official job description? But what do you actually do?
It’s potentially the most important question you can ask yourself if you care about standing out, staying ahead of the change curve, and continuously elevating your performance to gain access to choice assignments and opportunities to advance.
This is because the value you deliver, the results you produce, and the impact you have on others come more often from the execution of unspoken intangibles that are not reflected in your title, job description, or the daily tasks and activities you’re responsible for. This severe mismatch is based on a fundamental misunderstanding of the true demands of work.
Nobody told you this, but the day you were hired you actually accepted two jobs. The first was the position you interviewed for, including all of the tasks outlined in that job description. The second “job-within-the-job” included the unspoken, unwritten work that, among other challenges, requires you to manage constant change, collaborate well with others, navigate workplace politics, and get your best work done in an environment of shrinking resources and increasing demands. Nobody trained you to succeed in this hidden work, and you have to learn how to confront its everyday pitfalls. And although you can reach out to trusted colleagues for input, the pace of work and pressure to perform often limit our willingness to reflect, formulate questions, and take the time to seek guidance.
Nobody told you this, but the day you were hired you actually accepted two jobs.
As if this isn’t difficult enough, staying relevant at work requires you to get ahead of the change curve by steadily increasing your skills and abilities and finding innovative ways to go beyond your job description to add new value to your organization. These two elements combined — the challenges of your job-within-the-job plus the need to add value to your organization through continuous learning and performance — represent what I call the hidden curriculum of work.
The term hidden curriculum was coined by the educator Philip Jackson in 1968, and then elaborated upon by MIT’s Benson Snyder in 1970. Both explored the concept within the realm of education and youth development. I applied a new, expanded definition of the term to the workplace in my post-graduate research beginning in 2006.
A hidden curriculum exists whenever there are two simultaneous challenges where one is visible, clear, and understood and the other is concealed, ambiguous, and undefined. Take, for example, the lives of professional athletes. They must master the fundamentals of their sport and excel at the highest level on the court or field, but they also have to learn how to navigate murkier waters like wealth, fame, and other distractions that can arise. Similarly, when children enter school, they have to master their academic curriculum but, reading, math, and science do not prepare them for peer pressure, social dynamics, and developmental challenges of youth.
In the same way, we all encounter a hidden curriculum of work, regardless of tenure, level, or role. Whether you acknowledge it or not, you’re navigating your own hidden curriculum.
If leaders are responsible for equipping others to succeed on the job, trial and error just isn’t good enough. For example, when a leader tells his team, “We’re getting complacent and need more innovative ideas, so I want to encourage more debate at our weekly meetings,” he needs to recognize the hidden curriculum in this request. Encouraging debate can trigger defensiveness, which inadvertently shifts people into “advocacy mode”: an unconscious effort to prove a point, which inhibits listening, mental flexibility, and learning. When this happens, the capacity to stay curious, ask questions, and make connections among previously unconnected things is lost, and the intended result of the debate collapses.
Despite the complexities of such situations, the hidden curriculum of work can be identified and understood. What’s more, I believe that one of the most significant competitive advantages for organizations is a leadership group — and ultimately a workforce — that has the capacity to recognize the hidden curriculum of work and take deliberate steps to manage it. Considering this, the urgent questions for any employee are: Do you know your own hidden curriculum of work, and are you navigating it with focused attention? If you are a manager, do you know the pitfalls and demands of those who report to you, and are you taking proactive steps to equip them to address them?
Unfortunately, as “do more with less” has become the corporate world’s mantra, the rush to oversimplify distracts from these questions and the nuanced answers they bring. Perhaps it shouldn’t be surprising that one of the most common barriers (pdf) in advancing to and succeeding in a senior leadership role is an inability to switch from task execution (focusing on the tactical side of delivering work) to big-picture, strategic thinking (the ability to know what’s important, why it matters, and how to navigate the uncertainties in between).
Said another way, a valuable strength is the ability to shift from just getting the job done to actively observing and navigating the hidden side of work. Although there are no shortcuts to going beyond the job description, the next installment in this series will outline practical strategies to achieve this ability.

How to Set Up a Virtual Meeting Using Zoom

Step 1: Sign Up and Create an Account
To use Zoom, you need to have an account. If you don’t have one yet, go to the Zoom website and sign up. You will receive a confirmation email that you need to verify before you can log in.

Step 2: Schedule a Meeting
To schedule a meeting, log in to your account and click on the “Schedule a Meeting” button on your dashboard. Fill out the necessary details, such as the date, time, and duration of the meeting. You can also set up a recurring meeting if necessary. Then, click on the “Save” button.

Step 3: Invite Participants
After scheduling a meeting, you can invite participants by clicking on the “Copy Invitation” button. Step 4: Configure the Meeting Settings
Before you start a meeting, configure the meeting settings to suit your needs. You can do this by clicking on the “Settings” button on your dashboard. Here, you can set up options such as enabling or disabling the video, enabling or disabling the waiting room, and others.

Step 5: Start the Meeting
When it’s time to begin the meeting, click on the “Start Meeting” button on your dashboard. Participants can join the Zoom meeting by clicking on the link you shared with them or by entering the meeting ID and password.

Step 6: Troubleshooting
If the audio or video is not working properly, check your connection and settings. You can also try calling into the meeting using your phone. If you have connectivity issues, try restarting your internet router or using a wired connection instead.

Zoom is a great platform for virtual meetings. By following these steps, you should be able to set up and run a successful virtual meeting with ease. Remember, if you encounter any issues, don’t hesitate to reach out to Zoom’s customer support for assistance.

The legal systems of western Europe, with the exception of Great Britain, are based on Roman law and are called civil-law systems. Even the common-law tradition found in the English-speaking world has been influenced by it. In the United States, the Common Law has been paramount, but Roman law has influenced the law of the state of Louisiana, a former French territory that adopted a French civil-law code.
Roman law steadily accumulated during the course of the empire, and over time it became contradictory and confusing. In the early sixth century a.d., the Byzantine emperor Justinian I, appointed a commission to examine the body of law and determine what should be kept and what should be discarded. From this effort came the Corpus Juris Civilis, a Codification of Roman law that became the chief lawbook of what remained of the Roman Empire.
The decline of the Roman Empire also led to the diminution of interest in Roman law in western Europe. The Corpus was unknown to western scholars for centuries. During the twelfth century, however, Roman law studies revived in western Europe. In the late eleventh century, a manuscript containing part of the Corpus was discovered in Pisa, Italy. The remainder of the compilation was soon recovered, and schools where Roman law could be studied were established in Bologna, Italy, and then elsewhere in Europe. By the twelfth century, commentaries on the Corpus Juris Civilis appeared, and in time men trained in Roman law found posts in secular and ecclesiastical bureaucracies throughout Europe.
As a result, the legal systems of the Catholic Church and of almost every country in Europe were influenced by Roman law. Around the year 1140, the scholar Gratian prepared the Concordance of Discordant Canons, or Decretum. The Decretum was the largest and best-organized compendium of canon (church) law up to that time. It’s best to change the strings one at a time so that the tension exerted on the neck doesn’t fluctuate too much.
Loosen the string using the tuning machine. If you have a string winder, this is much faster. Pull the end out of the tuning post and clip the bent portion. This leaves the string tip straight so that it can be easily pulled out through the bridge by the ball end. Wrap and discard. Needlenose pliers can be useful here for extraction, especially if one of your strings has broken and a curly fragment is lodged in the post of the tuning peg.
Unwrap the fresh string and insert the straight end through the appropriate hole in the bridge. With a Stratocaster-style bridge, this insertion point is accessed under the panel on the back of the guitar. On other guitars with front-mounted tailpieces, such as Les Pauls, the insertion points are found at the back of the tailpiece just behind the bridge. Pull the string all the way through until the ball end catches securely.
In most acoustic guitars, the strings are held in place by small pegs called bridge pins. You can remove them using a coin or a pick for leverage, or with special tools found in almost any music store. Feed the ball end about halfway down the peghole and insert the pin, lightly pulling up on the string until you feel it wedge snugly. The goal is to trap the ball end between the narrow tip of the peg and the wall of the cavity. If pulling on the string pops the peg out of place, start over. It takes a little practice to get the feel for this, but you’ll pick it up quickly.
Pull the string all the way through the appropriate string post until it is taut, then pull it back out about one or two fret lengths to create some slack. Then kink it around the string post to set the length and tighten, counterclockwise, until your tuner indicates the desired pitch. A string winder speeds this process, but be careful not to overtighten as the string may snap. As the string wraps around the post, guide the protruding string end so that the coils sit nicely on top of and around it, keeping it secure. Clip the excess length from the post and discard.
The string, under tension for the first time, will naturally drop in pitch. To condition it, fret the string with one hand at the 12th fret. With the free hand, place a thumb against the guitar for leverage and use your fingers to gently pull the string up and down about an inch from the body for 15-20 seconds. The pitch will drop significantly; tune it back up to the correct note and repeat.

Introduction

With the advancement in technology, mobile payments have emerged as a revolutionary concept that has transformed the payments industry. Mobile payments are digital transactions that enable the transfer of funds from one account to another through mobile devices. This technology has surged in popularity globally and is characterized by its convenience, speed, and security. This report analyzes the ways in which mobile payments have revolutionized the payments industry, including their benefits and potential drawbacks, examines the challenges that businesses face in adopting mobile payments, and provides relevant statistics, case studies, and expert opinions to support the arguments.

Benefits of Mobile Payments

Mobile payments have had several benefits in the payments industry, including convenience, speed, and security. First, mobile payments offer convenient payment solutions as users only need their mobile devices to execute transactions, unlike traditional banking where customers must visit a bank branch or ATM to make payments. Additionally, mobile payments offer a fast and secure way of executing transactions. Mobile transactions are fast, safe and secure because they adopt cybersecurity measures such as end-to-end encryption, tokenization, multi-factor authentication, and virtual private networks to ensure customers' privacy and safety.

Second, mobile payments have revolutionized the payments industry by providing a cheaper payment method. Mobile payments are less expensive compared to traditional payment methods that involve the use of cheques, cash, or debit and credit cards. Mobile payments are typically associated with lower transaction costs, which make them more cost-effective for both merchants and consumers. An analysis conducted by the World Bank Group (2021) found that traditional payment methods cost $4.61 per transaction on average, whereas mobile payments cost $0.12 per transaction, making them significantly cheaper.

Third, mobile payments offer greater accessibility to financial services, especially to the unbanked and underbanked segments of society. Mobile payments allow individuals to transact and access digital financial services without being physically present at a bank branch. The technology has the potential to bridge the financial inclusion gap, particularly in developing countries where banking infrastructure is underdeveloped.

Potential Drawbacks of Mobile Payments

Despite having several benefits, mobile payments come with potential drawbacks that could potentially hinder their widespread adoption. One of the main drawbacks of mobile payments is network connectivity. Mobile transactions require a stable data connection to execute a successful transaction. Therefore, network connectivity issues and poor coverage can hamper the seamless execution of transactions, especially in remote areas where network coverage is poor.

Second, security concerns remain a significant drawback of mobile payments adoption. As the popularity of mobile payments rise, so does the risk of fraud, data breaches and hacking, which could lead to users' loss of money or sensitive data. Cybercriminals use sophisticated hacking techniques to gain access to mobile devices and steal personal information, such as bank account details, which could be used for financial fraud. Therefore, emphasis must be placed on enhancing the security of mobile payments to prevent fraud and secure customer data and privacy.

Business Challenges in Adopting Mobile Payments

Businesses have generally faced several challenges in adopting mobile payments, including security concerns, infrastructure requirements and customer adoption. First, implementing and upgrading infrastructure to accommodate mobile payments can be costly for businesses. Infrastructure requirements include purchasing mobile point-of-sale terminals, installing software and hardware, and training staff to effectively handle mobile payments.

Second, businesses face a significant challenge convincing customers to adopt mobile payments. Although mobile payments are efficient and cost-effective, it may be challenging to change the customer's behavior and adopt new payment methods. Therefore, businesses need to invest in programmatic marketing techniques to educate customers on the benefits of mobile payments, i.e., convenience, security, and lower transaction costs.

Lastly, businesses face a security challenge in adopting mobile payments. Due to the sensitive nature of financial data, businesses must implement advanced cybersecurity measures and protocols to protect customer data and prevent fraud. This requires significant investment in cybersecurity technologies and employee training to ensure all aspects of data security are addressed.

Conclusion

In conclusion, mobile payments have revolutionized the payments industry by providing convenient, fast and secure payment solutions. Mobile payments also offer cheaper payment transactions and increase financial accessibility to the unbanked and underbanked segments of society. However, network connectivity issues, security concerns, and technological infrastructure requirements remain potential drawbacks of mobile payments adoption. Sure, here's the step-by-step recipe for making a creamy and satisfying butternut squash risotto:

Ingredients:
- 1 medium-sized butternut squash, peeled, seeded, and diced into small cubes
- 1 onion, finely chopped
- 2-3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 1/2 cups Arborio rice
- 1/2 cup white wine
- 5-6 cups vegetable broth
- 1/2 cup grated Parmesan cheese
- 2 tablespoons butter
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- Salt and black pepper to taste
- Fresh herbs (e.g. Thyme, parsley, sage) for garnish

Instructions:

1. Heat the vegetable broth in a saucepan over low heat and keep it simmering on the stove.

2. In a large frying pan or dutch oven, heat the olive oil and butter over medium heat.

3. Add the chopped onion and sauté for 2-3 minutes until translucent.

4. Add the minced garlic and cook for another minute.

5. Stir in the Arborio rice and toast it for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly until the rice is coated with the oil and butter.

6. Pour in the white wine and stir continuously until it evaporates.

7. Add a ladleful of hot vegetable broth to the pan and stir until it's absorbed by the rice.

8. Repeat step 7, adding one ladleful of broth at a time, stirring constantly and waiting for the broth to be absorbed before adding more. Make sure the heat is at a medium-low level, so the broth doesn't boil too quickly.

9. After about 20 minutes, when the rice is almost cooked but still has a bit of a bite, fold in the diced butternut squash and continue stirring.

10. Add more broth as needed to keep the risotto from drying out, and cook for another 10-15 minutes until the squash is tender and the rice is fully cooked and has a creamy texture.

11. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the grated Parmesan cheese.

12. Season with salt and black pepper to taste.

13. Let the risotto rest for a few minutes before serving, garnished with fresh herbs.

Tips and tricks:

- It's essential to use Arborio rice, which is a short-grain rice that absorbs liquid well and releases starches as it cooks, giving risotto its characteristic creaminess.
- Don't leave the risotto unattended while cooking – it needs constant stirring and attention to ensure perfect consistency.
- If you prefer a richer and sweeter flavour, you can roast the diced butternut squash in the oven with a drizzle of oil, salt and pepper, before folding it into the risotto.
- You can also add some chopped spinach or kale at the end, for extra nutrition and colour.
- Leftover risotto can be stored in the fridge for up to 2-3 days and reheated on the stove with a splash of broth or cream to restore its creaminess.

response:
Static testing refers to a set of software testing techniques that are designed to identify defects in software without executing it. Such testing does not involve the execution of the software, instead involves examining the software code, documentation or artefacts, as well as the requirements and design specifications to highlight possible defects. These techniques come with practical advantages, limitations, and suitability for different stages of the software development life cycle. The techniques include review, walkthroughs, inspections, and static analysis.

Review Technique
The review technique involves a group of persons that examines documents, code, design, and requirements in search of errors, omissions, and ambiguities. It can be used in early stages of software development. Its advantages include generation of a better understanding of the design specifications, enhancing team communication and provides an inexpensive way of identifying issues in software development. However, its main limitation is the fact that the success of the review heavily depends on the experience and expertise of the team. Review is not suitable for detecting syntax errors and typos, but for identifying logical and conceptual errors in software.

Walkthrough Technique
Walkthrough is a technique where designers or developers walk through the software code with one or two other persons to find possible deviations from expectations. This technique is very useful in the initial design phase, as it allows the team members to identify gaps, inconsistencies and oversights. Walkthroughs have an advantage of providing a comprehensive understanding of the software design stage, enable team members to share knowledge and ideas, and quickly identify design flaws. However, it is not suitable for finding all defects, only significant issues that can be identified with a limited number of reviewers.

Inspections
Inspections is a formal method of non-executional testing of software artefacts which relies on a peer review process that allows the team to detect defects in the software by improving the quality of the work products. One of the benefits of inspections is that it helps reduce the cost of testing by detecting defects early, and enhancing software quality assurance through the removal of design errors before the implementation. On the contrary, inspections require additional resources, including time and money. Inspections are ideally suitable for QA procedures, detection of logical and conceptual errors, and improvements in the underlying architecture, as well as maintainability.

Static Analysis
Static analysis refers to the process of automatically scanning or reviewing code or other software artefacts to identify certain types of defects. Technical tools are used for this purpose to enhance software verification and quality. One of the major advantages of static analysis is that it is scalable, and can be used for large-scale development projects. Additionally, the technique detects coding errors that can be missed in other static testing techniques. The limiting factor, however, is that static analysis cannot analyse dynamic aspects of software, like execution path and memory management. Static analysis is suitable for detecting logical or implementation errors, implementation, and documentation aspects of software development.

In conclusion, each of the static testing techniques described above, including review, walkthrough, inspection and static analysis, can detect different types of software defects, depending on the stage of software development, and the type of errors that are being targeted. Therefore, it is critical for software developers to understand the strengths and weaknesses of each technique and apply them judiciously.

1. Select an appropriate location: ideally, the compost bin should be placed in a sunny area with good drainage.

2. Choose the right type of bin: there are several types of compost bins available, from diy to store-bought options. Some popular types include a tumbling bin, a stationary bin, and a worm composting bin.

3. Layer the materials: successful composting requires a good balance of greens (nitrogen) and browns (carbon) materials. The ideal ratio is 2:1 brown to green materials. 5. Turn the pile: turning the pile helps circulate the air and speed up the composting process. Use a pitchfork or shovel to turn the pile every 2-3 weeks.

6. Consider adding worms: worm composting, also known as vermicomposting, is a great way to speed up the composting process. Add a layer of worms to your bin, and they will help break down the materials.

In Greek mythology, time was personified by the god Chronos, who was often depicted with a serpent or dragon tail, reflecting the cyclical nature of time. Chronos was the god of time and was worshipped by the Greeks as the master of the universe. He was believed to have created the universe and was responsible for controlling the destiny of all living things. The different types of coral reefs found around the globe are:

1. Fringing reefs: These are the most common type of coral reefs and are found close to the shore. They grow along the coastline and are separated from the shore by a shallow lagoon.

2. Barrier reefs: These are similar to fringing reefs but are larger in size and are separated from the shore by a deep lagoon.

3. Atoll reefs: These are circular or ring-shaped reefs that grow around a lagoon. They are often formed on top of a submerged volcanic island.

4. Patch reefs: These are small and isolated reefs that are found in deeper waters.

The threats faced by coral reefs from climate change and human activity include:

1. Ocean acidification: The increased acidity of the ocean due to higher levels of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere can cause coral reefs to dissolve and die.

2. Climate change: Rising sea temperatures can cause coral bleaching, which can lead to the death of coral reefs.

3. Pollution: Human activity can introduce pollutants such as oil, chemicals, and plastic into the ocean, which can harm coral reefs.

4. Overfishing: Overfishing can lead to the destruction of coral reefs by removing the fish that help to protect them from algae and other predators.

5. Coastal development: The development of coastal areas for tourism, agriculture, and other purposes can lead to the destruction of coral reefs by dredging, land reclamation, and pollution.

Introduction

Cloud computing is a technology that provides remote access to computing services over the internet. It allows businesses and individuals to store, manage, and process data without having to invest in expensive hardware and software. The adoption of cloud computing has had a significant impact on modern businesses and their operations. This essay aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of how the advent of cloud computing has affected modern businesses and their operational processes. It will highlight the key advantages and potential drawbacks of cloud computing, notable trends, innovations, and emerging technologies within the field.

Advantages of Cloud Computing

One of the most significant advantages of cloud computing is that it provides businesses with a more cost-effective way of storing data and computing resources. Rather than having to invest in expensive hardware and software upfront, companies can rent space and services from cloud computing providers on a pay-per-use basis. This allows businesses to save money on capital expenses and reduce their overall IT costs.

Another advantage of cloud computing is that it provides businesses with more flexibility and agility regarding their IT resources. Cloud computing services can be scaled up or down as needed, depending on business requirements. This means that businesses can quickly respond to changing demands and adjust their IT resources accordingly. For example, a business may need to increase its computing resources during peak periods or to support a new project or initiative.

Cloud computing also allows businesses to improve collaboration and communication between teams and employees. Cloud-based tools such as file-sharing services, messaging platforms, and project management software enable teams to work more effectively together, regardless of their location or time zone.

Potential Drawbacks of Cloud Computing

Although cloud computing offers many advantages, there are also potential drawbacks that businesses need to be aware of. One of the main concerns is data security. Storing sensitive data in the cloud can pose a significant risk, as it is potentially vulnerable to cyber-attacks and data breaches. Therefore, businesses need to ensure that they have robust security measures in place to protect their data.

Another potential drawback is downtime. If a cloud provider experiences technical difficulties, this can result in downtime for its customers. This can have significant implications for businesses that rely heavily on cloud computing services. Therefore, businesses need to ensure that they have backup plans in place in case of downtime.

Notable Trends, Innovations, and Emerging Technologies

One of the most significant trends in cloud computing is the increased adoption of multi-cloud environments. This involves using multiple cloud providers to meet the different needs of a business. For example, a business may use one provider for application hosting and another for data storage. This approach can help businesses avoid vendor lock-in and ensure that they have access to the best services and technologies from multiple providers.

Another important trend is the increased use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in cloud computing. These technologies can be used to automate many tasks and processes, such as security monitoring, resource allocation, and predictive analytics. This can help businesses improve efficiency and reduce costs.

Other emerging technologies include serverless computing, which allows businesses to run code without having to manage servers, and edge computing, which provides local computing power near the devices that generate data.

Conclusion

Cloud computing has had a significant impact on modern businesses and their operational processes. It offers many advantages, including cost savings, flexibility, and improved collaboration. However, businesses need to be aware of potential drawbacks such as data security and downtime. Notable trends in cloud computing include multi-cloud environments, the use of AI and ML, and emerging technologies such as serverless computing and edge computing. As cloud computing continues to evolve and mature, businesses will need to stay up-to-date with the latest developments and innovations to remain competitive and successful.

How to Prepare a Delicious and Nutritious Smoothie Bowl

Smoothie bowls are a delicious and healthy way to start your day. They're loaded with nutrients and fiber, and they can be topped with all kinds of tasty and satisfying ingredients. In this guide, we're going to show you how to make a basic smoothie bowl, and then we'll give you some tips for customizing it to your taste and dietary needs.

Step 1: Choose Your Base

The first step in making a smoothie bowl is to choose your base. You can use any type of fruit or vegetable that you like, but some of the most popular options include bananas, berries, and greens like spinach and kale. Here are a few ideas to get you started:

- Berry Banana Smoothie Bowl: 1 banana, 1/2 cup blueberries, 1/2 cup strawberries, 1/2 cup almond milk
- Green Smoothie Bowl: 1 banana, 1 cup spinach, 1/2 cup kale, 1/2 cup almond milk
- Pineapple Mango Smoothie Bowl: 1 cup frozen pineapple, 1/2 cup frozen mango, 1/2 cup coconut milk

Step 2: Add Your Protein

Adding a source of protein to your smoothie bowl can help keep you feeling full and satisfied throughout the morning. Here are a few protein-rich ingredients you can add to your smoothie base:

- Greek yogurt
- Silken tofu
- Protein powder
- Nut butter

Step 3: Blend Until Smooth

Once you've added your base and protein, blend everything together until it's smooth and creamy. You may need to stop the blender and scrape down the sides a few times to make sure everything is fully incorporated.

Step 4: Layer Your Bowl

Now it's time to create your smoothie bowl masterpiece. Start by pouring your smoothie into a bowl, then add your favorite healthy toppings. Here are a few ideas to get you started:

- Fresh fruit
- Nuts and seeds
- Coconut flakes
- Granola
- Chia seeds

Customization Tips

Here are a few tips for customizing your smoothie bowl to your taste and dietary needs:

- Make it vegan: Use a non-dairy milk and skip the yogurt. Silken tofu is a great vegan protein option.
- Make it gluten-free: Use gluten-free oats or granola as a topping.
- Add healthy fats: Avocado, nut butter, and coconut oil are all great sources of healthy fats that can make your smoothie bowl more filling and satisfying.
- Experiment with flavors: You can add spices like cinnamon and ginger, or try using different types of fruit and vegetables to create new and interesting flavor combinations.

Conclusion

Making a delicious and nutritious smoothie bowl is a fun and easy way to start your day off on the right foot. By following these simple steps, you can create a customized bowl that's packed with nutrients and flavors you love. So go ahead and give it a try – your taste buds (and your body) will thank you!

Introduction

Alzheimer's disease is a progressive condition that affects cognitive functioning and memory, making it difficult for patients to communicate or perform basic daily activities. Music therapy has shown promise as a complementary intervention for individuals with Alzheimer's disease, due to its unique ability to engage various brain regions and promote positive emotional responses. This research article aims to explore the potential benefits, limitations, and risks associated with music therapy in Alzheimer's patients, as well as provide recommendations for integrating it into dementia care plans.

What is Music Therapy?

Music therapy involves the use of music, in various forms, to address emotional, cognitive, and physical needs of individuals. It is an evidence-based modality that aims to improve quality of life, reduce stress, and promote overall wellbeing. During music therapy sessions, a certified music therapist works to identify the patient's preferences and create a tailored plan to meet their unique needs. The sessions may include singing, playing musical instruments, movement, listening to music, or songwriting, among other activities.

Potential Benefits of Music Therapy in Alzheimer's Patients

Several studies have reported positive outcomes associated with music therapy for Alzheimer's patients. Music has been shown to have a positive impact on cognitive functioning, memory, mood, and overall quality of life. In a recent randomized control trial, researchers examined the effect of music therapy on cognitive functioning in people with Alzheimer's disease. The study found that participants who received music therapy had significantly improved scores on a cognitive assessment scale compared to the control group (1). Additionally, music therapy has been shown to reduce agitation, aggressiveness, and improve sleep quality among individuals with Alzheimer's disease (2).

Studies have also reported positive emotional responses and social engagement in Alzheimer's patients who participated in music therapy sessions. Music has the unique ability to evoke memories, emotions, and create a sense of connection between the patients and their caregivers. Participants in music therapy sessions are often observed singing along, tapping their feet, or playing instruments, which fosters socialization and interaction with others.

Limitations and Risks

There are some potential limitations and risks associated with music therapy for Alzheimer's patients. First, not all patients may respond positively to music therapy, and it may not be effective for everyone. In addition, the effectiveness of music therapy may depend on the patient's stage of the disease, severity of symptoms, and other individual factors. There is also a risk of overstimulation, particularly in patients with anxiety or agitation, which may lead to distress or unwanted behavior.

Recommendations for Healthcare Professionals

Based on the available evidence, music therapy can be a valuable addition to dementia care plans. Healthcare professionals are encouraged to consider integrating music therapy into their treatment plans for Alzheimer's patients. To get started, it is recommended that they work with a certified music therapist who can create a tailored program based on the patient's needs and preferences. Patient-centered care and communication with family members or caregivers are critical to ensure that the interventions are appropriate and effective.

Conclusion

Music therapy is a promising intervention for Alzheimer's patients, with various benefits that could improve their quality of life. Despite some limitations and risks, its potential for promoting cognitive functioning, reducing agitation, and fostering social interaction demonstrates its value. Future research should further investigate the mechanisms underlying the effectiveness of music therapy for Alzheimer's patients and explore the most effective ways of administering this modality. It is recommended that healthcare professionals incorporate music therapy as an alternative or complementary treatment to standard care.

(2) Zeng, X. J., Lei, L., & Guo, Q. (2021). The effect of music therapy on cognitive functioning of Alzheimer’s disease: A randomized controlled trial. BMC Geriatrics, 21(1), 1-7.

The first scientific mission with Sentry, a newly developed robot capable of diving as deep as 5,000 meters (3.1 miles) into the ocean, has been successfully completed by scientists and engineers from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) and the University of Washington (UW).
The vehicle surveyed and helped pinpoint several proposed deep-water sites for seafloor instruments that will be deployed in the National Science Foundation (NSF)'s planned Ocean Observatories Initiative (OOI).
Sentry is a state-of-the-art, free-swimming underwater robot that can operate independently, without tethers or other connections to a research ship.
The autonomous underwater vehicle, or AUV, is pre-programmed with guidance for deep-water surveying, but it can also make its own decisions about navigation on the terrain of the seafloor.
"This investment into emerging technologies is paying off in delivering state-of-the-art science support," said Julie Morris, director of NSF's Division of Ocean Sciences. "In the near future, Sentry will conduct high-resolution oceanographic surveys that would be otherwise impossible."
Working in tandem with sonar instruments on the UW-operated research vessel Thomas G. Thompson and with photo-mapping by WHOI's TowCam seafloor imaging system, Sentry gathered the most precise maps to date of seafloor features known as Hydrate Ridge and Axial Volcano off the coast of Oregon and Washington.
"We are changing the way ocean science is done, launching a new era in which an ensemble of technologies will provide us with an increasing capacity for exploring and interacting with the global oceans," said John Delaney, chief scientist of the expedition and principal investigator for the UW-led regional observatory in the planned OOI.
The one-of-a-kind, WHOI-built AUV--which was largely funded by NSF--made six dives during the July 22 to August 5 expedition.
Sentry surveyed 212 linear kilometers of seafloor, or about 53 square kilometers, as it traced parallel lines like a lawn-mower making a pattern across a yard.
"Sentry had a very successful introduction," said Dana Yoerger, the lead WHOI engineer for the vehicle. "We had tested the AUV as best we could before we got out here, but the steep terrain of the deep sea is quite a different matter."
The AUV can collect the data needed to make seafloor maps at a resolution of less than one meter. On this first cruise, Sentry collected as many as 60 million individual soundings of seafloor depth in a single dive.
Powered by more than 1,000 lithium-ion batteries-similar to those used in laptop computers, though adapted for extreme pressures, Sentry dove for as long as 18 hours and 58 kilometers, with the potential for longer trips in the future.
Sentry is designed to swim like a fish or fly like a helicopter through the water. The sleek hydrodynamic design allows the vehicle to descend quickly from the sea surface to the depths (about 3,500 meters per hour). The novel shape also gives the vehicle tremendous stability and balance while cruising through bottom currents.
The vehicle has thrusters built into its foils, or wings. Like an airplane, the foils allow the vehicle to gain lift or drag or directional momentum, as needed.
